TIMBER YARD AND INN IN FIRE AT KINGSTON-ON-THAMES. Aug 13

A large timber yard, an inn and two cottages on the riverside at kingston were involved in a great fire on Saturday Aug 11th. It broke out at dawn and raged for many hours. Earges were in flames and were towed out by a tug, the crew taking a great risk in keeping them from other craft. Kingston Bridge was closed to traffic until shortly before noon.

SCUTTLED--BLAZING BRITISH STEAMER'S END AT SEA. 281226.

An heroic losing fight with fire at sea was ended by the scuttling of the British steamer Airshire 200 miles from Ceylon. Several ships rushed to her aid in response to S.O.B. signals and her crew were taken off after battling with the flames. H.M. sloop Lupin played streams of water on the blazing vessel and took her to tow, but the flames spread and efforts to save her had to be abandoned.

By RUBY M. AYRES.

Sometimes they went for long walks; sometimes they took Jen's boat and rowed round the lifts to the sandy dove beyond; sometimes they only sat side by side on the sea-wall and talked. The prophecy of Signis had come surprisingly true. Peter was perfectly happy in Sleepy Hollow. He had even got accustomed to the hard mattress on his bed, and he had never felt so well in all his life. For the moment London was forgotten.
"And I've only known you three days," he aid to Eve Carteret soberly.
He was lying on his back beside her on the farm sand, staring up at the blue sky.
"Three days is a long time," she told himIPPantly. "I had a friend who got engaged and married in three days."
"The wonderful Dolly?" Peter inquired ab-ently.
He had heard so much about Dolly; he was a little tired of her name and a little sceptical as her charms of which Eve was never tired of telling him.
"Dolly isn't married," said Eve soberly. Poor Dolly," she added. "I have had a letter him her—she's very unhappy."
"She hardly seems what one would call a poorer person, does she?" asked Peter. He rolled over on his side, propped his bows in the loose sand and his chin in his ends.

"What's the matter with her now?" he in-
uired.

He was not really interested to know, but he anted Eve to go on talking; he liked the way her face lit up when she spoke of this wonderful friend of her's—though, if the truth must be told, he was more than a little jealousy of er. It seemed such waste of affection, he ought.

because the man must have been an utter fool, I should think, not to realise how altogether sweet she is. She's a girl in a thousand. I should like to meet the man who dared to do it. I'd pay him out."
'Ever had told him so little about herself and her life—she always seemed to keep deliberately to generalities, though she had long since extracted from him all about his brother and Dawson Towers.
He felt himself getting red; he rolled over again on his back, and this time tilted his hat so that none of his face was visible.
He did not even know as yet where her home as and what her people were. He wished she ad been as ready and willing to speak of them as she was of the everlasting Dolly.
Eve did not answer his question for a moment; she was absently sifting the dry sand through her fingers—her face looked a little trave.
"Good heavens" said Peter.
"Why!" the girl echoed scornfully. "Why.
He was conscious of a little twinge that eemed to run down his spine. He sat up and tilted his straw hat over his eyes.
Peter stared stonily out to sea. He thought of Angela Barton and the kisses and sweet nothings he had given and said to her; a fellow feeling made him wondrous kind towards this unknown sinner.

"I don't see how you can blame the man," he objected. "I suppose he discovered that he didn't care enough about her. Surely it's far better to own up and end it all than go on and marry her, and both be miserable for the rest of their lives."
"It's the way he did it that's so—so abominable," the girl protested hotly. "He just went off without saying good bye—only left a cowardly letter."
"Oh, my hat!" said Peter.

"I wish I knew who the man was," Eve continued fiercely. "Dolly won't even tell me his name, poor darling! She's dreadfully upset, and says she shall never care for anyone else. Care for him, indeed!" she echoed scornfully. "I think I'd kill a man who dare treat me like that."
Peter made no comment; he was watching her furtively from under his brim.
Suddenly she raised her grey eyes to his face. "She's been jilted," she said tragically.
Eve laughed.
"Thanks, very much," said Peter dryly. He did not at all relish the idea of a third corner to disturb this altogether delightful friendship.
"You'd like Dolly awfully," Eve went on, unconscious of his sarcasm. "And, anyway, you'll soon see for yourself, for she's on the way now."
"I wrote off to her at once," Eve went on, "and told her to come straight down here to me, and I'd soon make her forget him. You might help me," she added, smiling down at him. "You'd like Dolly."
"I don't like the sound of her name," Peter objected. "It sounds—silly, somehow. Dolly! Ugh!"

He laid a big hand over one of hers with sudden daring. "Tell me," he said again softly. She looked down at the long fingers covering hers with a little conscious flush before she drew her own slowly away.

For these are days when we live at open windows, or on balconies, or in back gardens—sit for a breath of air as far as possible in the open. We painfully notice, then, what noises are carefully cultivated for our distress by neighbours, or chance persons who come near us.

CAPTAIN HURLEY'S FLIGHT
Next month Captain Frank Hurley will lead another expedition into the wilds of Papua.

The story of the aerial exploration of this strange and savage country, which should make fascinating reading, will appear exclusively in New South Wales in "The Sun," and it will be illustrated by the wonderful photographs which have helped to make Captain Hurley famous. Below, Captain Hurley describes his plans.

It has for some time past been an open secret that I intend leading a second expedition into the heart of New Guinea with the object of exploring that unknown region from the air. I am now able to state that, through the generosity of Mr. Lebbeus Horndern, who has placed two seaplanes at my disposal, the expedition will leave for Papua next month. The patronage of the public to the pictorial record of my last expedition—"Pearls and Savages"—has enabled me to equip and finance the new undertaking.

FROM SEA TO SEA.
Two British Exploration Parties to Start Next Year.

Aeroplanes and sledges driven by aeroplane propellers are to play a big part in two important expeditions to the Antarctic—the frozen continent where Captain Scott and his heroic companions triumphed and perished.
Plans are now being made by Sir Ernest Shackleton—who will be making his third trip to the Antarctic—and Mr. J. Foster Stackhouse, the leaders of the expeditions.

Sir Ernest Shackleton intends to start with the Imperial Trans-Arctic expedition next year, his aim being to march night across the South Polar continent from Weddels Sea to McMurdo Sound. The expedition will have two ships.
Mr. Foster Stackhouse's expedition will leave for the Antarctic next August, and he hopes to chart and survey the huge King Edward VII, land discovered by Captain Scott in his first expedition.
"The British Empire," in the words of Sir Ernest Shackleton, "has lost during the last three years the premier place she held in polar exploration, and now is the chance to recover that prestige."

"In any case, I shall have two ships, one to take us to Weddels Sea and the other to await us in Ross Sea."

"If we are doing very well we shall make for McMurdo Sound direct. And if we are doing very well indeed, and our aeroplane sledges are in good order, we may perhaps strike further north.

CAPTAIN SCOTT'S GREAT TASK.

Captain Scott reached the South Pole on January 18, 1912, and there found that Captain Amundsen had arrived before him. Then began the tragic march back, which ended in the death of the whole party on March 25.
The first to die was Seaman Edgar Evans, who perished on February 17 at the foot of the Beardmore-Glacier.

The party, already in distress, struggled bravely on. Captain Oates suffered from frostbite and bore intense pain without complaint. Then he bravely walked out of the little tent to his death. "The act," as Captain Scott wrote, "of a brave man and an English gentleman."

Three were still left, and they were overtaken by a blizzard, only a few miles from safety. Food and fuel failed them, and Captain Scott, Lieutenant Bowers and Dr. Wilson died together in the little tent, where, on November 10, 1912, their bodies were found by the search-party sent after them.

There also was found Captain Scott's last hero message, in which he denies regret for the journey, which had shown that "Englishmen can endure hardship, help one another, and meet death with as great fortitude as ever in the past."
